claims.text: Controlled thermal annealing can increase lattice distortion in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Increasing lattice distortion through annealing increases dislocation network density.
Lattice distortion raises local energy barriers to dislocation motion.
Higher barriers to dislocation motion increase yield strength.
Dense dislocation networks alter local stress distributions under thermal loading.
Dislocation-induced changes in local stress distribution moderate thermoelastic strain during high-temperature operation.
Additional annealing will produce a statistically significant increase in high-temperature yield strength relative to the unannealed baseline.
Additional annealing will produce a distinct, moderated thermoelastic strain response relative to the baseline.
Baseline samples without the additional anneal will have lower lattice distortion than treated samples.
Baseline samples without the additional anneal will have lower dislocation density than treated samples.
The proposed mechanism is applicable during mechanical loading and thermal cycling above 900 °C.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
In situ neutron diffraction can monitor lattice parameters and provide an assessment of dislocation density during the proposed tests.
Diffraction peak shifts or broadening can be used to quantify lattice distortion.
TEM or diffraction analysis can be used to quantify dislocation density.
Dislocation-mediated deformation is relevant to the mechanical behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Local chemical order may influence the relationship between lattice distortion and mechanical response.
Using identically composed and baseline-processed control and treated samples is intended to isolate the effect of the additional annealing treatment.
Failure to observe both increased yield strength and moderated thermoelastic strain in the higher-distortion samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Attribution of the apparent improvements to microstructural changes other than lattice distortion and dislocation density would falsify the proposed causal mechanism.
